items.readable_text:
Content:
Two expressions are equivalent if they always have the same value, even if they look different.

Content:
A useful way to check whether two expressions are equivalent is to simplify each one. If they can be written in the same form, they are equivalent. This often involves using techniques like distributing, collecting like terms, or factoring.

Content:
For example, let's check if [MATH: 2(3x+4)] and [MATH: 8x+8-2x] are equivalent.

Content:
The first expression, [MATH: 2(3x+4),] is already simplified in a factored form. We will now simplify the second expression, [MATH: 8x+8-2x,] to see if we can get it into the same form.

Content:
First, we simplify the second expression by collecting like terms:
[MATH: 8x + 8 − 2x|=; 8x − 2x + 8|=; (8 − 2)x + 8|=; 6x + 8]

Content:
Then, we factor out the greatest common factor. Since [MATH: \text{GCF}(6x,8)=2,] we get
[MATH: 6x + 8|=; (2 ⋅ 3x) + (2 ⋅ 4)|=; 2(3x + 4)|.✓]

Content:
The simplified form, [MATH: 2(3x+4),] matches the first expression.

Content:
Since the expressions can be written in the same form, they are equivalent.

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following expressions is equivalent to [MATH: 4(3x-7)?]

  1. [MATH: 12x-28]

  2. [MATH: 5x-7-2x]

  3. [MATH: 6x+6x-32]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following expressions is equivalent to [MATH: 4(3x-7)?]

1. [MATH: 12x-28]
2. [MATH: 5x-7-2x]
3. [MATH: 6x+6x-32]

sections.normalized_html:
To determine which of the expressions are equivalent to [MATH: 4(3x-7),] we first collect like terms and then factor each result:

  • We factor out the greatest common factor in expression I. Since [MATH: \text{GCF}(12x,28)=4,] we get [MATH: 12x − 28|=; (4 ⋅ 3x) − (4 ⋅ 7)|=; 4 ⋅ (3x − 7)|.✓] So, expression I is equivalent to [MATH: 4(3x-7).]

  • There are two like terms in expression II, [MATH: 5x] and [MATH: -2x.] Combining these terms, we have [MATH: 5x − 7 − 2x|=; 5x − 2x − 7|=; (5 − 2)x − 7|=; 3x − 7.] Now, we factor out the greatest common factor. Since [MATH: \text{GCF}(3x,7)=1,] there is nothing to factor out. [MATH: 3x - 7 \qquad{\color{red}\times}] So, expression II is not equivalent to [MATH: 4(3x-7).]

  • There are two like terms in expression III, [MATH: 6x] and [MATH: 6x.] Combining these terms, we have [MATH: 6x + 6x − 32|=; (6 + 6)x − 32|=; 12x − 32.] Now, we factor out the greatest common factor. Since [MATH: \text{GCF}(12x,32)=4,] we get [MATH: 12x − 32|=; (4 ⋅ 3x) − (4 ⋅ 8)|=; 4 ⋅ (3x − 8)|.×] So, expression III is not equivalent to [MATH: 4(3x-7).]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".
